summary: The best-supported explanation (H2, confidence 0.60, medium) is a demand-side capacity saturation of auth-service: a genuine ~3.8x step in inbound login traffic beginning ~06:50Z overwhelmed auth-service's fixed worker pool (64) and maxReplicas 8, filling the accept queue and producing ~4s p99 latencies and 503s. The competing retry-amplification hypothesis (H5, 0.18) is weakened by ordering evidence at both api-gateway and auth-service: request volume climbs monotonically from ~06:49-06:50Z while error rates and p99 stay at baseline for another ~4-5 minutes, the reverse of the retry-after-failure order H5 requires. The reporter's bcrypt-regression theory (H1) is refuted — no auth-service deployment exists anywhere in April 2026 — and the shared-redis (H3) and dependency-stall (H4) hypotheses are excluded on timing, flat dependency metrics, and the accept-queue-full (not downstream-timeout) 503 signature. Confidence is capped at 0.60 (not higher) because the origin of the demand surge cannot be attributed to a specific caller, region, or tenant: the decisive instrumentation (per-caller log fields, retry/attempt metrics) does not exist, so the "genuine external demand vs. edge/client regeneration" hop remains an assumption rather than a verified fact.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Demand step: ~3.8x surge in login requests saturates auth-service capacity (retry storm / caller burst)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A demand-side event began around 06:50Z, stepping requests to POST /v1/auth/login from ~395 to ~1500 req/s (and api-gateway inbound from ~1250 to ~4900 req/s). auth-service's fixed worker pool (64) and maxReplicas 8 cannot absorb it, so the accept queue fills, CPU pins at ~97%, and 503s are returned. Load preceded errors and latency at both the gateway and auth-service, which is what a genuine demand step (rather than retry regeneration) produces. The origin is the demand source itself; whether that source is an external client burst or client/gateway retries cannot be attributed because auth-service and gateway logs carry no caller/region/tenant/cid field.
ranked_hypotheses.root_cause_service: auth-service (demand-side origin: external caller / client burst; source unattributed)

causal_chain.claim: A demand-side event (external caller burst) begins around 06:50Z — no attributed source could be identified (log records carry no caller/region/cid: F33)

api-gateway inbound request_rate climbs first and monotonically from ~1212 (06:49) to 2165 (06:52), then ~4871-4955 req/s sustained; it is NOT a pass-through of auth-service's count (~3.2x differential)
auth-service request_rate steps ~3.8x from ~395 to ~1500 req/s at 06:50Z (plateau from 06:55)
Gateway latency and 5xx stay at baseline through 06:53 and only jump at 06:54-06:55 — load precedes errors, i.e. demand drives the failure, not retry-after-failure
auth-service CPU saturates (~97%) and worker pool fills (active=64/64, queue=39035); gateway CPU stays flat 37-46% with zero WARN+ logs, so upstream is not resource-limited
Accept queue fills; 503 'accept queue full' returned on /v1/auth/login; autoscaler cannot scale past maxReplicas 8; rate limiting only steps at 06:55, after the load step
p99 rises to ~3.8s and error rate to ~14%, gateway reflects the same latency/5xx, persisting to end of data

assumptions: The inbound request surge is genuine inbound demand and not an artifact or internal amplification (per-caller attribution was unobtainable: F33)
No proactive scaling or effective inbound rate limiting existed to absorb the surge
The source is external to auth-service, since no change event sits near onset (F15)

ranked_hypotheses.title: Client/gateway retry amplification regenerates login calls, self-sustaining the overload after an initial trigger
ranked_hypotheses.statement: An initial transient latency blip on the login path caused clients or the api-gateway to retry POST /v1/auth/login; each retry adds load, multiplying effective demand ~3.8x and self-sustaining the overload. The origin is retry/amplification behaviour at the client or gateway layer, not auth-service code. This is now WEAKENED by ordering evidence: load rises BEFORE errors/latency at both gateway (F38/F39) and auth-service, which is the reverse of what retry-after-failure requires. It remains active only because retry amplification cannot be directly measured (no retry metric: F40) and no per-caller attribution exists (F33).

causal_chain.claim: An initial latency blip on the login path triggers client/gateway retries — assumed; no blip precedes the load step (pre-onset p99 is a flat ~90ms baseline for auth-service, ~200-214ms for gateway)
Retries are counted as fresh inbound requests; api-gateway request_rate rises to ~4900 req/s and auth-service to ~1500 req/s
Gateway load precedes gateway errors/latency (error_rate and p99 flat until 06:54-06:55) — the opposite ordering from what retry regeneration predicts
auth-service worker pool (64) and maxReplicas 8 cannot absorb the multiplied load; accept queue fills; 503 on /v1/auth/login feeds further retries
Sustained ~4s p99 and ~14% 5xx through end of data; rate limiting steps only at 06:55, after the load step

assumptions: The surge is concentrated in retries rather than uniform organic growth (per-caller/tenant attribution was never obtained: F12 truncated, F33 no cid/region field)
Login callers or the gateway retry on 503/latency (no retry metric or retry config was observable: F40)

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared dependency (user-db / redis-cache) or external kyc-provider degrading beneath auth-service
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A dependency of auth-service on the login path degraded, so auth-service request handling blocked, occupying worker threads and consuming CPU, producing queue saturation and 503s. REJECTED: its required signature is absent — no downstream timeout/connection-pool/DB errors appear in auth-service logs (all 503s are accept-queue-full, F11); user-db shows flat CPU (~18%) and flat slow_queries (F28) and its connections step is coincident with, not preceding, onset (F27); redis-cache hit_ratio and evictions are flat through onset (F25, F26); user-db neither stalls nor saturates (F28, F30).

causal_chain.claim: A dependency (DB, cache, or kyc-provider) degrades or stalls on the login path — no dependency-side degradation observed
auth-service request handling blocks on the dependency, occupying worker threads
Worker pool saturates (active=64/64) and CPU pins high
Accept queue fills; 503 'accept queue full' on /v1/auth/login
p99 ~3.8s and ~14% 5xx persist

assumptions: A dependency actually degraded (no dependency-side metric shows a stall)
The failure mechanism would produce accept-queue-full 503s rather than downstream timeout errors
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Required downstream-failure signature absent: auth-service logs contain no timeout/connection-pool/DB errors — every 503 is 'accept queue full' application overload (F11, F36); user-db cpu flat ~18% and slow_queries flat (F28); redis-cache hit_ratio and evictions flat through onset (F25, F26); user-db connections step is coincident with, not preceding, onset (F27). The kyc-provider branch is unobservable (F29, has_telemetry false) rather than disproved, but H4-as-framed requires a downstream timeout signature that does not exist.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Bad deployment in portfolio-service v4.4.0 (dep-5803) degrades the shared redis-cache, amplifying auth-service login path
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The only change in the window, dep-5803 (portfolio-service v4.4.0, CSV export endpoint, 05:50Z), introduced a workload that degrades the shared redis-cache — which auth-service also depends on — indirectly harming the login path, causing queueing on auth-service. REJECTED on timing and metrics: a 1-hour quiet gap between the deploy and the 06:50Z step (F15); redis-cache hit_ratio and evictions flat through onset (F25, F26); redis-cache and api-gateway have zero config changes (F17); other shared consumers show no change events (F20-F23); and auth-service's failure is accept-queue-full overload, not dependency latency (F11).

causal_chain.claim: dep-5803 adds a CSV export endpoint that reads/writes the shared redis-cache heavily
Shared redis-cache degrades (latency/miss/eviction) affecting all consumers incl. auth-service — no such degradation observed
auth-service login path slows and CPU saturates as work backs up
Worker pool saturates and 503s issued on /v1/auth/login

assumptions: redis-cache actually degraded as a result of the portfolio deploy (contradicted by flat redis metrics)
Degradation would only manifest in auth-service, not equally in the other shared consumers
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Timing: the 05:50Z deploy is ~1h before the 06:50Z step with a clean quiet interval (F15). Mechanism: redis-cache hit_ratio (94.9-97.4%) and evictions (1.2-4.4/min) show no step at or before onset (F25, F26); redis-cache and api-gateway have zero config changes (F17); other shared consumers (pricing-engine, market-data-service) have zero deployments/config changes (F20-F23). auth-service's signature is accept-queue-full overload, not dependency latency (F11). A redis-mediated mechanism is excluded regardless of the other consumers' unretrieved telemetry.

ranked_hypotheses.title: bcrypt cost regression from an auth-service release (reporter's theory)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A recent auth-service release reintroduced the bcrypt cost-factor regression, making login CPU-bound and slow. REFUTED: there is no auth-service deployment in any queried window (all of April), the only auth-service config change is a log.level tweak 3h10m before onset, and the HIST-101 precedent's trigger condition (a release) is absent.

causal_chain.claim: An auth-service deployment raising bcrypt cost factor occurs (as in HIST-101) — no such deploy exists
Each login hash becomes CPU-bound, driving CPU saturation
Worker pool saturates, queue fills, 503s returned on /v1/auth/login
p99 steps from ~90ms to ~3.8s and error rate to ~14%

ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: No auth-service deployment exists in all of April (F1, F3, F13); the only auth-service config change is log.level INFO->WARN 3h10m before onset with no bcrypt setting (F2, F14); the HIST-101 precedent requires a release trigger that is absent (F18). CPU saturation is accompanied by a genuine ~3.8x demand step (F10), not the standalone per-hash CPU cost HIST-101 produced.

facts.statement: auth-service p99 latency shows a step change between 06:50Z and 06:55Z, from a ~90 ms baseline to 3770-3868 ms, sustained through 08:50Z — a step, not a ramp.
auth-service 5xx error_rate steps from ~0.18-0.25% baseline to 7.11% in the 06:50Z bucket and a sustained ~13.8-14.1% from 07:00Z onward.
auth-service CPU saturates at onset, moving from 38-40% baseline to ~96.6-98.3% between the 06:50Z and 06:52Z buckets, and remains pinned at ~97%.
auth-service request_rate steps ~3.8x at onset: ~383-405 req/s baseline through 06:40-06:45Z, then sustained ~1450-1540 req/s; this is a demand/load step, not merely a latency symptom.

All 503s in auth-service are application-level accept-queue-full rejections on POST /v1/auth/login ('request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503'), preceded by 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=39035)' and an autoscaler warning that desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; no connection-pool, timeout, or DB errors appear in auth-service logs.
Every auth-service error is concentrated on the single endpoint POST /v1/auth/login; the log query was truncated (40 of 372), so per-region/tenant/caller attribution was not determined.

api-gateway request_rate steps up at the same onset: ~1245-1264 req/s through the 06:36Z bucket, then 2846.83 avg (max 4859.74) at 06:48Z and ~4871-4955 req/s from 07:00Z onward; the gateway did not stay flat.

api-gateway latency_p99 and 5xx step up in lockstep with auth-service: p99 was 206-214 ms through 06:36Z, then ~2068 ms at 06:48Z and ~3877-3961 ms from 07:00Z; error_rate was 0.19-0.22% through 06:36Z, then ~3.95% at 06:48Z and ~8.9-9.2% sustained.

Load precedes errors at the gateway: request_rate climbs monotonically from 06:49Z (1212.38) through 06:52Z (2164.64) while error_rate stays at baseline (0.12-0.31%) until it jumps at 06:55Z — a ~4-5 minute gap in the H2 order, not the retry-after-failure order.
Gateway latency_p99 confirms the same ordering: flat at ~200-211 ms through 06:53Z, jumping to 4024.51 ms at 06:54Z, ~5 minutes after request_rate began climbing.
api-gateway is far from resource-saturated during the load step: cpu_pct stays flat at 36.9-46.0% and it produced zero WARN-or-above log entries in 06:30-07:15Z.

auth-service rate_limited_per_min is flat at ~0.8-2.9 req/min through the pre-onset and load-ramp period (06:48Z 1.37, 06:50Z 2.22, 06:52Z 1.38, 06:54Z 1.66) and only steps ~500x to 902.06 at 06:55Z — after the load step and coincident with the 503 onset.

No auth-service deployment exists in the entire month of April 2026; the only deployment across all services in the 2026-04-21T00:00Z to 2026-04-22T08:59Z window is dep-5803 (portfolio-service v4.4.0, CSV export endpoint) at 2026-04-22T05:50Z.

The only config change anywhere in the window is cfg-2801: auth-service log.level INFO->WARN at 2026-04-22T03:40Z, containing no bcrypt/cost-factor/worker-pool/connection-pool setting, ~3h10m before onset.

The HIST-101 bcrypt precedent (2025-08-14) requires an auth-service release as its trigger ('bcrypt cost factor raised 10->14 in release v6.4.0'); no auth-service deployment exists this time, so the precedent's trigger condition is absent.
redis-cache hit_ratio_pct shows no step across 06:30-07:10Z, staying within a narrow 94.9-97.4% band, and evictions_per_min fluctuate only 1.17-4.42 keys/min with no eviction surge.
user-db does not show a query-stall signature: slow_queries_per_min stays ~0.2-0.5 with no step and cpu_pct is flat ~17-19% across the entire window.
user-db connections_active shows a sharp step in the 06:52Z bucket (~26 through 06:50Z, then 73-82), coincident with — not preceding — the auth-service onset.

redis-cache is flagged shared:true and is consumed by auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service; redis-cache and api-gateway have zero config changes over 2026-04-15 to 2026-04-22T08:59Z.

The other shared redis-cache consumers show no change events in the bracketing window: pricing-engine and market-data-service have zero deployments in 05:00Z-08:59Z and zero config changes in 00:00Z-08:59Z.
No retry/attempt/re-request metric exists on either api-gateway or auth-service (exposed metric sets contain no retry or attempt counter), so retry amplification cannot be measured directly.

api-gateway request_rate is ~2.7-3.2x auth-service's own inbound request_rate in identical 60s buckets both before and during onset (baseline 06:44Z: gateway 1300.06 vs auth 392.25; post-onset 06:59Z: gateway 4859.74 vs auth 1813.74), with no accepted explanation from telemetry.

auth-service log records carry no caller, region, tenant or correlation-id field: a log query for 'region' over 06:40-07:10Z returned total_matched 0, so per-caller attribution of the surge is structurally unavailable.
kyc-provider has no telemetry at all (has_telemetry false, no logs/metrics), so external-provider latency cannot be measured directly.

The shared-dependency hypothesis lacks its required signature: all 503s are accept-queue-full application overload rather than downstream timeout/connection-pool errors, redis hit_ratio/evictions are flat, and user-db CPU/slow-queries are flat.

assumptions: The inbound request surge is genuine inbound demand and not an artifact or internal amplification; per-caller attribution was unobtainable (F33) and no retry/attempt metric exists (F40).
The demand source is external to auth-service, since no change event sits near onset (F15) and no auth-service deployment exists in April (F1, F3, F13).
No proactive scaling or effective inbound rate limiting existed to absorb the surge: autoscaling was capped at maxReplicas 8 (F11) and rate_limited_per_min did not step until 06:55Z (F41, F44).

The ~2.7-3.2x gateway-to-auth request-count differential (F37) reflects genuine demand/amplification rather than differing metric semantics (routed/authenticated calls, health checks, keep-alive multiplicity); telemetry cannot resolve this.

Whether the demand step originates from external clients, a client/gateway retry loop, or an unmeasured upstream (e.g. kyc-provider-driven retries) cannot be attributed with available instrumentation.

auth-service is running an unknown version with no observed change since before 2026-04-01; the absence of a bcrypt code/config diff is from absence of deployment evidence, not a positive version check.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) No change event sits within minutes of the 06:50Z onset: the portfolio-service deploy predates onset by ~1 hour and the auth-service log-level config change by ~3h10m.

timeline.event: Prior incident HIST-101: bcrypt cost factor raised 10->14 in auth-service release v6.4.0 produced identical symptoms (login p99 4s, 503 on login, high CPU); resolved by rollback. Its required trigger (a release) is absent in the current incident.
Sole config change in the window: cfg-2801 changes auth-service log.level INFO->WARN ('Reduce log volume'); contains no bcrypt/cost-factor/worker-pool setting; ~3h10m before onset.
Sole deployment in the window across all services: dep-5803, portfolio-service v4.4.0 (CSV export endpoint) by ci-bot; ~1 hour before onset. No auth-service deployment in April.
api-gateway begins stepping up: request_rate 1245-1264 req/s baseline through 06:36Z then ~2847 avg (max 4859.74); p99 and error_rate remain at baseline (p99 206-214 ms, error ~0.2%) at this point.
Gateway request_rate climbs monotonically (1212.38 at 06:49Z) while gateway error_rate stays at baseline 0.12-0.31% — load precedes errors.

auth-service demand and resource step: request_rate jumps ~3.8x from ~390-405 req/s to a sustained ~1450-1540 req/s; p99 steps from ~90 ms to 3770-3868 ms; error_rate steps to ~14%; CPU rises to ~97%.
auth-service CPU reaches ~96.6-98.3%; user-db connections_active steps from ~26 to 73-82, coincident with (not preceding) onset; redis-cache hit_ratio and evictions remain flat.

gateway latency_p99 jumps from ~211 ms to 4024.51 ms — ~5 minutes after request_rate began climbing; auth-service begins emitting 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=39035)' warnings from 06:54:53Z.

503 onset: first 'request rejected: accept queue full' login 503s from 06:55:42Z; gateway error_rate jumps to 9.4%; auth-service rate_limited_per_min jumps ~500x (1.66 -> 902.06) — throttling follows the overload rather than preceding it.
Autoscaler warns 'desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' (also at 07:01:30Z), confirming the fixed capacity ceiling.
Incident INC-008 reported by on-call SRE; symptoms login latency ~4s and 503s on /v1/auth/login.

Latest data: auth-service p99 and ~14% error rate persist; CPU remains pinned ~97%; shared-dependency metrics (redis hit_ratio/evictions, user-db CPU/slow_queries) remain flat; redis-cache and api-gateway show zero config changes.

recommended_actions.action: Mitigate the overload now by adding auth-service capacity: raise the autoscaling ceiling (maxReplicas from 8 to at least the observed desired 14+) and/or increase the fixed worker pool above 64 — the exact autoscaler setting flagged in the 'desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' warning. This is the capacity ceiling identified in the incident; verify whether the current autoscaling setting is a named config item before changing it.
recommended_actions.rationale: H2 attributes the outage to demand (~3.8x surge to ~1500 req/s) exceeding a fixed 64-worker pool and maxReplicas 8, producing accept-queue-full 503s while CPU sits at ~97%. Raising the ceiling directly addresses the identified constraint.

recommended_actions.action: Verify H2-versus-H5 discriminator live: capture gateway request_rate, error_rate and latency_p99 alongside auth-service request_rate for the next 15 minutes and confirm that load continues to precede errors (the H2 order) rather than the reverse; if errors cannot be induced without a preceding volume rise, H5 is effectively excluded.
recommended_actions.rationale: H2 and H5 differ on the single unverified hop — whether the surge is genuine or retry-regenerated. The ordering signature (F38/F39) already favors H2 but was only observed once; a confirming or contradicting observation settles it.

recommended_actions.action: Apply inbound rate limiting / load shedding at api-gateway for POST /v1/auth/login (the endpoint carrying 100% of the 503s) to cap effective demand at auth-service while the capacity fix is applied, and instrument it so throttled requests are attributable.
recommended_actions.rationale: All errors are concentrated on POST /v1/auth/login (F12, F32). Existing throttling at auth-service only engaged after the accept queue was already full (F41, F44), too late to prevent saturation.

recommended_actions.action: Determine and document the origin of the demand step: identify the client/region/tenant/caller driving the ~3.8x login surge, using any data path that carries caller identity (e.g. gateway access logs or upstream CDN/edge records), since auth-service and gateway logs carry no caller/region/tenant/cid field.
recommended_actions.rationale: The root-cause hop is assumed, not verified: per-caller attribution was structurally unavailable (F33) and there is no retry/attempt metric (F40). Without it, the H2 origin cannot be fully closed out or H5 definitively excluded.

recommended_actions.action: Add per-caller/correlation-id attribution and an explicit inbound-rejection and retry/attempt counter to auth-service and api-gateway telemetry so the next occurrence can distinguish external demand from edge/client retry amplification.
recommended_actions.rationale: These are precisely the fields whose absence blocked attribution this time (F33, F40, F41), and they are the direct discriminator between the top two hypotheses.

recommended_actions.action: Add an auth-service dependency-stall guard: alert on downstream timeout/connection-pool errors and on user-db replication_lag_ms and redis-cache cpu_pct/connected_clients, since those specific signals were never retrieved; confirm after this incident that none were breached.
recommended_actions.rationale: H4 was rejected on the absence of a downstream-failure signature and flat user-db CPU/slow-queries and redis hit_ratio/evictions (F11, F25, F26, F28), but user-db replication_lag_ms, disk_used_pct and redis cpu_pct/connected_clients were never queried, leaving a residual blind spot on the dependency path.

recommended_actions.action: Plan capacity/redundancy for auth-service so a step-in-demand event of ~3.8x can be absorbed: raise maxReplicas and worker-pool sizing with load-tested headroom, and implement pre-emptive autoscaling or admission control rather than reactive scale-up.
recommended_actions.rationale: The acute failure was a demand step against a hard capacity ceiling (maxReplicas 8, worker pool 64) with autoscaling unable to respond in time — a structural gap regardless of the demand source.

recommended_actions.action: Reconcile the ~2.7-3.2x discrepancy between api-gateway and auth-service request counts (identical 60s buckets, both before and during onset) to establish whether they reflect genuine amplification or differing metric semantics.
recommended_actions.rationale: The unexplained differential (F37) is the one piece of evidence that could still be read as retry amplification; resolving it removes a lasting ambiguity between H2 and H5.

data_gaps: No per-caller/region/tenant/correlation-id attribution exists in auth-service or gateway logs: a query for 'region' returned total_matched 0, and the error-log result was truncated (40 of 372). Whether the ~3.8x step is concentrated in one caller/region (retry-storm signature) or uniformly broad cannot be determined; concentration is only inferable indirectly via the gateway's parallel step-up.

No retry/attempt/re-request/connection-multiplicity metric exists on api-gateway or auth-service, so retry amplification (H5) can only be inferred, never measured; the H2-vs-H5 discriminator is limited to ordering evidence.

The ~2.7-3.2x gateway-to-auth request-count differential (F37) has no accepted explanation; it could be retry amplification or differing metric semantics (routed calls, health checks, keep-alive), and telemetry cannot resolve which.

auth-service's currently deployed version is unknown — no deployment exists in April 2026 or wider windows, so the bcrypt hypothesis is refuted only by the absence of a deployment trigger, not by a positive code/config diff; a non-deployment configuration path for bcrypt cost was not ruled out.

user-db replication_lag_ms and disk_used_pct, and redis-cache cpu_pct and connected_clients, were never queried (tool budget exhausted), so a residual dependency-side cause cannot be fully excluded on all available metrics.

kyc-provider has no telemetry (has_telemetry false) and auth-service exposes no outbound-call latency/error metric, so an external-provider-driven retry storm generating the login surge cannot be measured or excluded.

No telemetry (metrics, logs, config changes, downstream edges) was retrieved for pricing-engine or market-data-service, the other shared redis-cache consumers; their 'unaffected' status rests only on absence of change events, not on their own telemetry.

Whether the 05:50Z portfolio-service v4.4.0 deploy produced any redis-cache load/latency effect around 05:50Z was never measured (no such metric exists and the budget ended), so a redis-mediated indirect link cannot be finally excluded from the data.
Metric buckets are aligned to the minute, so the gateway-load-leads-auth-load ordering has 60-second resolution and cannot be resolved to the second.

The exact autoscaling/worker-pool configuration item (e.g. the maxReplicas 8 and worker-pool 64 settings) was observed only via log warnings, not via a config inventory, so the precise change surface for mitigation should be confirmed before altering it.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Evidence that the 06:50Z request-rate rise was generated inside the edge/client layer rather than upstream of it — e.g. a gateway or client retry loop whose attempts are counted as new inbound requests, or a per-caller breakdown showing the surge concentrated in re-requests following latency — would move the conclusion from H2 to H5.
A pre-onset latency blip on the login path (before 06:50Z) would supply H5's required trigger and strengthen retry amplification over genuine demand.
Discovery of any unobserved change to auth-service (code, bcrypt cost factor, worker-pool sizing, or connection pooling) near onset would reopen H1 or H4.

A resumed or newly visible downstream-failure signature — connection-pool/timeout/DB errors in auth-service logs, a user-db slow-query or CPU step, or a redis hit_ratio/eviction/latency step at or before onset — would reopen H4.

Evidence that the 05:50Z portfolio-service v4.4.0 deploy degraded the shared redis-cache (e.g. a redis step at or before 05:50Z) or telemetry showing the other shared consumers also degraded would reopen H3.

A quantified explanation of the ~2.7-3.2x gateway-to-auth request-count differential as differential metric semantics (routed calls, health checks, keep-alive) would raise confidence in H2 by removing the last retry-amplification reading.
Confirmation that no external caller or upstream service actually increased login volume (e.g. all callers at baseline, no CDN/edge surge) would contradict H2's assumed root hop and force re-ranking.

findings.statement: Only one deployment occurred across ALL services in the 2026-04-21T00:00Z→2026-04-22T08:59Z window: dep-5803, portfolio-service v4.4.0 ('CSV export endpoint'), deployed 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z by ci-bot, status 'live', rolled_back_at null. No auth-service deployment appears.

Only one config change across all services in the same window: cfg-2801, auth-service key 'log.level' changed INFO→WARN at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z by config-bot ('Reduce log volume'). Its timing is ~3.4h before the incident report; nothing indicates bcrypt or cost-factor settings were changed.

Widening to 2026-04-15→2026-04-22T07:06Z returns the same single deployment (dep-5803) and same single config change (cfg-2801); a further auth-service-scoped query over 2026-04-01→2026-04-22T08:59Z returns count 0: no auth-service deployment in the entire month of April.

It requires an auth-service release as trigger — none exists this time.

findings.statement: auth-service topology: it depends on user-db (postgres), redis-cache (kind cache) and kyc-provider (external, has_telemetry false); api-gateway depends on auth-service (http). redis-cache is flagged shared:true and is also used by portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service.

The shared redis-cache is a plausible cross-service coupling: deployments found this window include portfolio-service (v4.4.0), which is itself a redis-cache consumer, and redis-cache is shared with portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service.

auth-service shows a step change in latency and errors between 06:50 and 06:55Z: p99 latency jumps from a ~90 ms baseline (steady ~88-91 ms avg across 05:00-06:40) to 3770-3868 ms avg (max 4081 ms) from the 06:50 bucket onward, and stays there through 08:50. The transition is a step, not a gradual ramp.

auth-service error_rate (HTTP 5xx) rises in the same step: baseline ~0.18-0.25% through 06:40, then 7.11% avg in the 06:50 bucket and a sustained ~13.8-14.1% (max 15.67%) from 07:00 onward. Errors persist to the latest data point.

auth-service CPU saturates at onset: 38-40% baseline through 06:50, then ~96.6-98.3% from 06:52 onward (2-min buckets show the jump between 06:50 avg 34.42 and 06:52 avg 96.89). CPU remains pinned at ~97% to the end.

auth-service request_rate jumps ~3.8x at onset: ~383-400 req/s baseline through 06:40, then avg 1078 (max 1813) in the 06:50 bucket and sustained ~1470-1520 req/s from 07:00 on. This is a demand/load step, not just a latency symptom.

503 error signature in auth-service is application-level overload, not a downstream dependency failure: 372 ERROR entries all match 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)', first seen 06:55:42Z. Preceded by WARN 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=39035)' from 06:54:53Z, and autoscaler WARN 'desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' at 06:57:15Z and 07:01:30Z. No connection-pool/timeout/DB errors appear in the auth-service logs.

findings.statement: All errors are concentrated on the single endpoint POST /v1/auth/login (every one of the 372 matched ERRORs carries that path); no other auth-service endpoint appears in the error patterns. Log query was truncated (returned 40 of 372), so per-region/tenant/caller attribution was not determined.

Across ALL services for 2026-04-21T00:00Z→2026-04-22T08:59Z there is exactly one deployment: dep-5803 portfolio-service v4.4.0, deployed 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z by ci-bot, changes ['CSV export endpoint'], status 'live', rolled_back_at null. No auth-service deployment exists, so no code-regression trigger is present.

The only config change anywhere in the same window is cfg-2801: auth-service key 'log.level' INFO→WARN at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z by config-bot ('Reduce log volume'). It contains no bcrypt/cost-factor/worker-pool/connection-pool setting, and its timestamp is ~3h10m before the 06:50Z onset.

The change timeline does NOT coincide with the 06:50Z step change: the single portfolio-service deploy at 05:50:00Z predates onset by ~1 hour and the auth-service log-level config change at 03:40:00Z predates it by ~3h10m. Onset was 06:50-06:55Z (p99 90 ms→3770-3868 ms; error_rate 0.2%→~14%; request_rate ~395→~1500 req/s per T1), i.e. no change event sits within minutes of the step.

auth-service topology: it depends on user-db (db) and redis-cache (cache), plus external kyc-provider (has_telemetry false); api-gateway depends on auth-service (http). redis-cache is the only node flagged shared:true, and it is also used by portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service — exactly the component through which the 05:50Z portfolio-service v4.4.0 deploy could couple to the login path.

The shared-dependency leads have no supporting change events of their own: redis-cache has zero config changes over 2026-04-15→2026-04-22T08:59Z and api-gateway likewise has zero config changes over the same window. The only shared-component-adjacent change is the portfolio-service deploy on the shared redis-cache's consumer side.

The 'bcrypt regression' precedent (HIST-101, 2025-08-14) matches on symptoms only (match_score 3/2: 'login p99 4s','503 on login','high cpu') but its root cause explicitly requires an auth-service release: 'bcrypt cost factor raised 10->14 in release v6.4.0', resolution 'Rolled back v6.4.0'. No auth-service deployment exists this time, so the precedent's trigger condition is absent — supporting that this is not a repeat. The closest non-release precedent HIST-115 (order-service pool exhaustion) is likewise a config change, of which there is none affecting pools here.

The only precedent involving redis-cache with another consumer (HIST-107, 2025-12-09) was a cold-cache storm after a redis failover with root cause 'Redis primary failure promoted an empty replica' — an infrastructure failure at redis itself, not a consumer-side change. It is a lead only, not evidence about the current incident.

findings.statement: redis-cache shows no step in hit_ratio_pct across 06:30-07:10Z: it stays in a narrow 94.9-97.4% band (e.g. 06:48 avg 95.41, 06:50 avg 96.80, 06:56 avg 94.91, 07:10 avg 97.05). No miss-rate deterioration at or before 06:50Z.

redis-cache evictions_per_min show no step: values fluctuate 1.17-4.42 keys/min throughout, baseline 2-3/min before onset (06:48 avg 3.35) and similar after (06:52 avg 3.08, 07:00 avg 3.6, 07:08 avg 3.88). No eviction surge.

user-db connections_active shows a sharp step starting in the 06:52Z bucket, NOT before 06:50: ~23-27 connections through 06:50 (06:50 avg 26.12), then 73.31 at 06:52, 79.1 at 06:54, sustained ~75-82 through 07:10. The jump is coincident with (not preceding) the auth-service onset.

user-db does NOT show a query-stall signature: slow_queries_per_min stays ~0.2-0.5 throughout (06:50 avg 0.29, 06:54 avg 0.41, 07:10 avg 0.51) with no step, and user-db cpu_pct is flat ~17-19% across the entire window (06:50 avg 18.78, 07:10 avg 18.02). The DB itself is not saturated.

kyc-provider has no telemetry at all: querying its latency returns 'kyc-provider is an external dependency: we have no logs/metrics for it' with caller auth-service. External-provider latency cannot be measured directly.

findings.statement: Metric-name discovery: user-db exposes only connections_active, cpu_pct, disk_used_pct, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min (no pool-saturation or query-latency metric); redis-cache exposes only connected_clients, cpu_pct, evictions_per_min, hit_ratio_pct, memory_pct (no explicit latency or ops metric).

auth-service request_rate steps ~3.8x at onset: ~390-405 req/s baseline 06:00-06:45, then 680.57 avg (max 1012.36) in the 06:50 bucket, 1475.5 avg (max 1813.74) at 06:55, and sustained ~1450-1540 req/s through 08:55. This is a demand step on the inbound side.

The FULL set of 'accept queue full' errors for POST /v1/auth/login over 06:30-07:10Z is 44 ERRORs, all matching the single pattern 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning <n> (POST /v<n>/auth/login)', first_seen 2026-04-22T06:55:42Z and last_match 2026-04-22T07:09:31Z (this query returned 40 of 44, total_matched=44, truncated). Every error carries the /v1/auth/login path; no other endpoint appears.

findings.statement: The error/warn log records contain NO caller, region, tenant or correlation-id field: the messages are only 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)' and 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=39035)'. A log query for 'region' in auth-service over 06:40-07:10Z returned total_matched 0.

api-gateway — queried explicitly by its real service name (available_metrics includes request_rate, latency_p99_ms, error_rate) — DOES step up at the same onset, it did NOT stay flat: request_rate ~1245-1264 req/s through the 06:36 bucket then 2846.83 avg (max 4859.74) at 06:48 and ~4871-4955 req/s from 07:00 onward.

api-gateway latency_p99 and 5xx step up in lockstep with auth-service: p99 was 206-214 ms through 06:36, then 2068.02 avg (max 4200.87) at 06:48 and ~3877-3961 ms sustained from 07:00; error_rate was 0.19-0.22% through 06:36, then 3.95 avg (max 9.4) at 06:48 and ~8.9-9.2% sustained. The gateway reflects the same ~4s latency and ~9% 5xx that auth-service shows.

The accept-queue / worker-pool saturation is application-level overload persisting beyond the incident report: WARN 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=...)' from 06:54:53Z with queue depths up to 98763, interleaved with the 503 ERRORs, all on the login path.

api-gateway request_rate is ~3.2x auth-service's own inbound request_rate in identical 60s buckets before and during onset — the gateway is NOT a pure pass-through of the count auth-service reports. Baseline 06:44: gateway 1300.06 avg vs auth 392.25 avg; 06:48: gateway 1243.59 vs auth 385.12; post-onset 06:59: gateway 4859.74 vs auth 1813.74. Ratio ranges ~3.2-2.7x across the window.

The gateway's request_rate rises FIRST, and its error_rate only follows ~4-5 minutes later. request_rate: 06:49 1212.38 → 06:50 1348.68 → 06:51 1652.95 → 06:52 2164.64 (monotonic climb from 06:50). error_rate over the SAME buckets stays at baseline: 06:48 0.12, 06:49 0.24, 06:50 0.30, 06:51 0.31, 06:52 0.18, 06:53 0.24, 06:54 0.16, and only jumps at 06:55 9.4. Load therefore precedes errors by ~4-5 min (H2 order), not the reverse (H5 order).

api-gateway latency_p99 confirms the same order: it is flat at ~200-211 ms through 06:53 (06:50 213.45, 06:51 204.03, 06:52 207.66, 06:53 211.62) and only jumps to 4024.51 at 06:54, i.e. ~5 min after request_rate began climbing at 06:50. Gateway latency degradation follows the load step, it does not precede it.

NO explicit retry/attempt/re-request metric exists anywhere in the observed metric sets. api-gateway exposes only cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts; auth-service exposes cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, rate_limited_per_min, request_rate, restarts. There is no upstream_requests-vs-retries, 5xx-triggered re-request, connection/attempt-count or per-connection multiplicity metric, so retry amplification cannot be measured directly — only inferred from the request-count differential in F-1.

The only retry-adjacent signal that exists, auth-service rate_limited_per_min, is flat at ~0.8-2.9 req/min for the entire pre-onset and load-ramp period (06:48 1.37, 06:50 2.22, 06:52 1.38, 06:54 1.66) and then jumps ~500x to 902.06 at 06:55, sustaining ~820-950 req/min thereafter. This step is coincident with the 503 onset (06:55) and the gateway error_rate jump (06:55), i.e. after the load step, not before it.

api-gateway itself is far from resource-saturated during the load step: cpu_pct stays flat at 36.9-46.0% (06:30 40.86, 06:50 42.39, 06:55 36.92, 07:15 40.06) and it produced ZERO WARN-or-above log entries in 06:30-07:15Z (total_matched 0). So the extra ~3.2x upstream volume is not explained by gateway-side CPU/connection strain and the gateway logs record no retry/error activity.

rate_limited_per_min IS present in auth-service's metric set (available_metrics: cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, rate_limited_per_min, request_rate, restarts). It is nonzero but very low (~0.8-2.9 req/min) for every minute 06:30-06:54Z, and shows NO step at 06:50Z. The values around the load step: 06:44 0.8, 06:48 1.37, 06:49 2.21, 06:50 2.22, 06:51 1.97, 06:52 1.38, 06:53 1.03, 06:54 1.66 req/min.

The only step in rate_limited_per_min occurs at 06:55:00Z, jumping ~500x from 1.66 (06:54) to 902.06 req/min, then sustaining ~820-950 req/min through 07:15Z. This is 5 minutes AFTER the 06:50Z load step and coincident with the 503 onset (F11/F32 first 503 at 06:55:42Z), i.e. the throttling is a consequence of the overload, not an earlier throttle of an external flood.

Zooming in to 2-minute buckets around onset confirms the ordering: 06:44 1.42, 06:46 1.83, 06:48 1.79, 06:50 2.1, 06:52 1.21, then 06:54 451.86 (max 902.06) and 06:56 870.12 — the step sits at 06:54-06:55Z, not at 06:50Z, so rate limiting does not precede or coincide with the onset of the load/request-rate rise.

Interpretation for the tie-breaker: no inbound throttling/rejection activity exists at or before 06:50Z, so there is no evidence of an unsolicited external flood being throttled (the H2-flood variant is NOT supported by this metric). The rate-limit step appearing only after the load/error step is weakly consistent with self-generated retry load (H5 direction). This is a weak, non-decisive signal and must be weighed against the gateway load-precedes-errors ordering (F38/F39), which points the opposite way (H2).
